crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

children.name: Drafting a Manuscript
children.blurb: Drafting a manuscript in academic writing and peer review covers the preparation of a complete research paper, from structuring the introduction, methods, results, and discussion to revising for clarity, argument, and citation integrity.

children.name: Testing Arguments Before Peer Review
children.blurb: Testing arguments before peer review means using structured critique to find weak premises, missing counter-evidence, and overclaimed conclusions in a manuscript before it reaches reviewers.

children.name: Disciplinary Register and Language
children.blurb: Disciplinary register and language refers to the specialized vocabulary, grammatical patterns, and rhetorical conventions that mark writing within a particular academic field, and how these conventions shape peer review.

children.name: Plagiarism and AI Detection
children.blurb: Plagiarism and AI detection in academic writing and peer review covers identifying copied text, paraphrased material, and machine-generated prose in manuscripts, student work, and grant proposals.

children.name: Explaining Research After Publication
children.blurb: Explaining research after publication covers the work of turning a published paper into accessible summaries, annotations, and discussions for readers beyond the original authors.

sections.body: This section covers how artificial intelligence is used in academic writing and peer review, from drafting manuscripts to testing arguments before submission, matching disciplinary register, checking originality, and explaining research after publication. In practice, AI tools now help researchers generate initial drafts, rephrase sentences, summarize literature, and format citations. They can also simulate reviewer questions or counterarguments to stress-test a paper before it is sent to a journal. Some systems compare text against large databases to flag possible plagiarism or AI-generated passages. After publication, AI assists with plain-language summaries and social media posts to help work reach wider audiences.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: The work is uneven. Drafting assistance is widely available and reasonably reliable for structure and language, but it cannot guarantee factual accuracy or novel argumentation. Testing arguments with AI can surface obvious gaps, yet it often misses subtle disciplinary objections or misreads the stakes of a field. Disciplinary register tools can adjust tone and vocabulary, but they may flatten an author's voice or misuse field-specific terms. Plagiarism and AI detection remain contested, with high false positive and false negative rates, and no detector is accepted as definitive. Post-publication explanation is improving, but AI summaries can oversimplify methods or overstate findings.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: A reader starting with Drafting a Manuscript will see how AI helps produce sections, manage references, and revise prose, while Testing Arguments Before Peer Review moves from writing to stress-testing the paper's logic and evidence. Disciplinary Register and Language addresses the harder problem of sounding like a member of a specific field, and Plagiarism and AI Detection covers the risks of originality checking and the limits of current detectors. Finally, Explaining Research After Publication closes the loop by showing how AI can turn a finished paper into accessible summaries for broader audiences. Together the pages follow a manuscript from blank page to public impact, with each page naming the tools and limits relevant to that stage.
